title: I Saw Three Ships
description: The traditional English carol to its Derbyshire tune, as Bramley and Stainer printed it in Christmas Carols New and Old, for 2 to 4 singers: four of its nine verses, the three ships, what was in them, the Virgin Mary and Christ aboard, and the last, "Then let us all rejoice amain". A lively 6/8 on Stainer's chords, the alto in sixths and thirds under the tune.

licence.words: public domain: traditional (the book's index gives the words' source as "Traditional"); the words editor Henry Ramsden Bramley died 1917
licence.tune: public domain: traditional (the index gives the air as "Traditional (Derbyshire)")
licence.arrangement: after John Stainer's four parts (the book's index: "Harm. by J. S."; Stainer died 1901; public domain), in his key of G. His tune as printed, except for the breaths (the tune has no rests): "day;" in the middle of each verse and "ing" at the end of verses 1 to 3 give up a quaver, and the pickup after each ("I", "And", "The", "Then") comes in a semiquaver late, so each breath is half a beat; and verse 3 sings "Ma-ry" on two quavers where the tune has the crotchet of "ships". His chords kept for most of the verse (the held G of the first bar with its passing D7, D and G under "sail-ing in, On", E minor and D under "saw three ships" in the second half, C under the last "day"), with a C chord over his held G under "mas day," and "mas" in the last line, a G chord over his held D under the middle "day;", D under the second "sail-" where he moves from G to D7 in quavers, and a D7 under "morn-" where he has D, with F sharp 2 in the bass (resolving to G) and the tenor falling to D3, so every size has its third and seventh. His bass kept in bars 3 to 5 and at the start of bar 7, an octave lower in the first bar, and moved to the chord's root where his high notes (B3, C4, D4) or a doubled F sharp would fall. Ours: the alto, which in Stainer holds D4 through the first four bars and sings the opening "I" in unison with the tune, rewritten in sixths and thirds under the tune so the duet and trio have a third from the first note; the tenor rewritten as a moving line that takes the notes the alto gives up; every part one note a syllable where his inner parts move in quavers under "sail-"; under "saw three ships come" in each verse's second half the alto sings E4, E4, F sharp 4, G4 in thirds under the tune and the tenor G3, B3, C4, B3, so the duet and trio have the D chord's third and the four-part D7's seventh falls to B; the bass moves to D3 on "come" in the first bar and holds it into "sail-", so the outer parts don't move into an octave by similar motion; breaths written in for beginners; accepted exceptions: the duet under "morn-" sings A4 over C4, the fifth and seventh of the D7 (the two-part cadence; F sharp in the alto would end every verse in unison), and the duet and trio go without F sharp under the first "ships", a passing chord over the held G (Stainer's chord there has none either). On the semiquaver pickup after the middle breath ("I", "And", "The", "Then" of each verse's second half) the alto keeps the B3 of "day;" over the D chord, so the duet and trio sing D and B there for a moment; the tenor has the F sharp.
licence.source: H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old (London: Novello and Company, Limited; New York: Novello, Ewer and Co.; the complete book of 70 carols, undated, its title page naming "Sir John Stainer"; catalogued [1880]), No. 64, "I saw three Ships", Briskly, pp. 164 and 165, in four parts in G, 6/8, written here in G in 6/8 as printed; the index (p. 182): "I saw three ships come sailing in", words "Traditional", air "Traditional (Derbyshire). Harm. by J. S."; verse 1 as printed under the music and verses 2, 3 and 9 as printed on p. 165 (sung here as verses 1 to 4); the page's second setting, "Or this (in 3 parts)" in F, is another tune and was not used; Brigham Young University copy, read from the scan at archive.org/details/christmascarolsn00lond/page/n169 and n170 (index n187). The same tune, in A, with the words of verse 1, is in William Henry Husk, Songs of the Nativity (London: John Camden Hotten, undated, catalogued [1884]), "Christmas Carol Tunes", p. 190, "On Christmas Day in the Morning", archive.org/details/cu31924073426169/page/n215; its harmony is not used
